title: Close reading an extract
examples: How can looking at just a small part help me understand the whole story?
What should I look for when I read a short passage from a book?
Does the beginning part always tell me everything about the end?

explain.say: Today we learn to read small parts closely.

items: Step 1: Focus on the small part
Step 3: Make connections and draw conclusions

explain.say: First we look closely at the details in the extract.
Next we think about what comes before and after this part.

items: The Extract: What is happening now?

explain.say: Then we consider the author's purpose for writing this section.
By doing this we move from the small piece to the whole story.
In real life we use this when reading news articles.

faq.q: Does close reading mean I should just summarize the passage?
faq.a: No, summarizing just tells what happened. Close reading looks at how the author wrote it to show meaning.
asks: Is it just retelling the story?
Should I just tell what the text says?

faq.q: How much evidence do I need to support my ideas?
faq.a: You need specific examples from the text. Pointing to exact words or phrases makes your reading strong.
asks: Do I need to quote everything I say?

faq.q: Should I worry about the author's background?
faq.a: Considering the context helps you understand why the author wrote it then. This adds depth to your analysis.
asks: Does history matter for this essay?
Should I research the author's life?

faq.q: What if the extract is confusing or unclear?
faq.a: That is okay. You can discuss the ambiguity. You can suggest multiple possible meanings based on the evidence.
asks: What if I don't understand it?
Can I say it means two things?

faq.q: Is there a difference between inference and evidence?
faq.a: Evidence is what the text shows you directly. Inference is what you logically guess based on that evidence.
asks: What is the difference between guessing and knowing?
How do I make an inference?

facts: Close reading involves analyzing specific textual features like diction and imagery.
Context refers to the background information surrounding the text's creation.
Inference is a conclusion reached on the basis of evidence and reasoning.
Analyzing an extract helps build an understanding of the entire work.

quiz.say: The author uses the word 'murky' instead of 'dark'. This focus on word choice is an example of:
quiz.why: Diction analysis looks at the specific word choice to understand the tone.

wrong.0: Context relates to time or place, not the word itself.
wrong.1: Inferring is guessing the meaning, while diction analysis points to the word.
wrong.3: Summarizing only gives the general meaning, not the specific word choice.

quiz.say: If an extract describes a character always looking over their shoulder, what literary device are you focusing on when you consider their paranoia?
quiz.why: Body language is a specific detail that reveals something about the character's inner state.

wrong.0: Setting is the time and place, not the character's actions.
wrong.1: Theme is the big idea, not the physical action shown.
wrong.2: A plot point is an event, but body language is a continuous detail.

quiz.say: When moving from an extract to the whole text, you must ensure that your conclusion about the theme is:

options.show: a prediction of what will happen
options.say: a prediction of what will happen

quiz.why: A strong conclusion must be backed up by evidence from different parts of the text.

wrong.0: You must consider details from the beginning as well.
wrong.1: While predictions are good, the conclusion must reflect what is already present.
wrong.3: Your opinion is not enough; the text must provide the support.
